paper_title: Label optimal regret bounds for online local learning
authors: Pranjal Awasthi, Moses Charikar, Kevin A Lai, Andrej Risteski
statement: Conjecture 2 Suppose that an algorithm A receives as input a graph G, which is either sampled 1 0 from the ensemble G(n, p) or G(n, p, k, q), where k = n 2 − for 0 = Ω(1) and k = nΩ(1) ; p = n−α for α = Ω(1), α ≤ 12 ; q = k −α− for  = Ω(1); and p = o(q). Then, no A which runs in polynomial time can decide with probability 54 which ensemble the input was sampled from.
context: To be formal, we conjecture the following: Conjecture 2 Suppose that an algorithm A receives as input a graph G, which is either sampled 1 0 from the ensemble G(n, p) or G(n, p, k, q), where k = n 2 − for 0 = Ω(1) and k = nΩ(1) ; p = n−α for α = Ω(1), α ≤ 12 ; q = k −α− for  = Ω(1); and p = o(q). Then, no A which runs in polynomial time can decide with probability 54 which ensemble the input was sampled from. There are few ways to justify this conjecture. First, the current best known algorithm for this Θ() distinguishing problem from Bhaskara et al. (2010) runs in time nk . This bound gives a running Θ() time of 2n since k is polynomial in n, which is significantly worse than quasi-polynomial. Second, it’s possible to show Bhaskara et al. (2010) that spectral methods do not work in this regime. 2. The constant is arbitrary. One could make the conjecture for any constant bounded away from 21 4
